rows.description: Starting cycling or returning after a break? Measure your starting position, check saddle and handlebar access, then test one change on an easy ride.

rows.quick: Quick answerBike fit for beginners starts with control, not a low racing position. An unfamiliar or old setup may not suit the riding you do now. Record your current position, check that you can brake safely, then compare one targeted change at a time during easy rides.
rows.article: The problem: bike fit for beginners You have bought a bike, borrowed one or taken your old bike out of storage. The first kilometres feel unfamiliar. You slide on the saddle, keep changing hand position or hold your arms rigidly. A short test ride may have felt fine, while the same position becomes uncomfortable on a longer outing. That makes starting confusing. You do not yet know what belongs to ordinary effort and what concerns the setup. Returning riders can feel uncertain too. An old position does not automatically feel comfortable after a lengthy break. You do not need to replace components immediately or copy an experienced rider's posture. Start by asking whether you can pedal, look ahead, steer and brake comfortably. This guide helps organise those first checks. Pain, tingling and lost sensation are not compulsory stages of getting used to cycling. Record when a problem starts rather than changing everything because of a vague impression. Background: getting used to a bike is not the same as fitting it Your position sits between the saddle, pedals and handlebar. Moving the saddle therefore changes more than its height alone. The distance to your hands may feel different too. One uncomfortable contact point does not immediately prove that one particular measurement is wrong. A borrowed bike still carries someone else's setup. On an old bike of your own, clothing, shoes and intended use may have changed. Perhaps you now prefer relaxed outings to fast group rides. Start with that present purpose rather than an old photograph. Frame size limits what you can adjust. Components also have their own installation limits. The Trek owner's manual, for example, warns that enough seatpost must remain inside the frame. A marking is not permission to move beyond it to reach a calculated ideal measurement. The ride itself also matters when assessing a position. A short, easy circuit is a different comparison from a demanding outing. If you ride further while adjusting components, it becomes harder to understand which change relates to your experience. Keep the first comparisons straightforward. You do not need a power meter to record your route, duration and impressions. Online tools can organise measurements and calculate an initial proposal. They cannot observe your braking or movement when you become tired. They do not investigate pain either. Ask a mechanic about uncertain installation and a fitter about persistent positioning difficulties. Medical symptoms belong with a clinician. These boundaries do not make a basic starting measurement less useful; they make its meaning clearer. How to approach it with bike fitting Make the bike safe first: Check tyres, brakes and component security according to the manufacturer's instructions. Do not use a ride to discover whether a loose handlebar will stay attached. Ask a mechanic if installation is uncertain. Check that you can operate the brakes from your normal hand position without sliding forwards on the saddle. Keep the starting position: Stand the bike upright on a level floor. Use a tape measure for saddle height. Measure from the centre of the bottom bracket to a consistent point on the saddle. Record that point and the measurement in millimetres. Take a side photograph and record saddle and handlebar positions so you can recover the original setup later. Calculate an initial comparison: Measure your body using the instructions in the bike fit calculator. Check the units and repeat any uncertain measurement. Treat the result as a proposal rather than a compulsory final position. A large difference from your current setup calls for checking the inputs and measurement method before making a change. Choose one understandable adjustment: Work only on a component that you know how to adjust safely. Record the old and new measurements, including the direction. No fixed millimetre step suits every beginner and every component. Remain within manufacturer limits and use the specified tools. Let a professional adjust an unfamiliar handlebar or saddle assembly instead. Compare two to three easy rides: Use a familiar route and similar effort while you remain symptom-free. Record whether pedalling, braking and looking ahead become easier. Note new pressure points too; a better saddle sensation is not the whole result. Return to the recorded safe position if things worsen. Do not finish a testing series at the expense of pain. Recognise the limit of self-testing: Stop for lost sensation, radiating tingling or symptoms that reduce your control of the bike. Seek medical assessment for pain at rest or at night, swelling or persistent symptoms. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, consult a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. A new bike is never a reason to ignore warning signs while trying to settle into cycling. Further reading Bike fit and body proportions explains why a friend of the same height does not provide a reliable personal starting position. Bike frame size helps check whether the bike offers enough adjustment room for your riding position. Saddle height expands the first saddle measurement before you start changing other contact points. Handlebar width and hood position helps assess safe hand contact without immediately buying a different handlebar. Cycling power and pacing helps keep effort during comparison rides deliberate and straightforward to record. The bike fit calculator gathers your body measurements and offers an initial proposal to assess on the bike. Frequently asked questions Do I need special cycling shoes for my first setup? No. Record the shoes and pedals you currently use and compare your first rides with those. Different shoes can change the starting conditions. Recheck your position when you switch rather than changing shoes, saddle and handlebar together. You do not need a complete new equipment collection to investigate one unclear discomfort. Can I use my old saddle position when returning to cycling? You can record it as a starting point if the installation is safe. It does not prove that the same position still suits your current rides. Start gently and check brake access, pedalling and comfort again. Change something only when you have a clear reason and a safe way to compare it. Should I always reach the ground with both feet flat? Do not use that as the only measure of saddle height. The bike type and how you mount and dismount also matter. Ask for help if stopping feels uncertain. You need to stop and get off safely, but saddle position must also be assessed while you pedal. Is a free calculation enough before I attempt longer rides? A calculation is a beginning, not a declaration that everything is correct. Check the proposal during easy rides and build experience with your own bike. Ask for help if the position remains uncertain or symptoms develop. mainEntity.name: Do I need special cycling shoes for my first setup?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Record the shoes and pedals you currently use and compare your first rides with those. Different shoes can change the starting conditions. Recheck your position when you switch rather than changing shoes, saddle and handlebar together. You do not need a complete new equipment collection to investigate one unclear discomfort.

mainEntity.name: Can I use my old saddle position when returning to cycling?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can record it as a starting point if the installation is safe. It does not prove that the same position still suits your current rides. Start gently and check brake access, pedalling and comfort again. Change something only when you have a clear reason and a safe way to compare it.

mainEntity.name: Should I always reach the ground with both feet flat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not use that as the only measure of saddle height. The bike type and how you mount and dismount also matter. Ask for help if stopping feels uncertain. You need to stop and get off safely, but saddle position must also be assessed while you pedal.

mainEntity.name: Is a free calculation enough before I attempt longer rides?

acceptedAnswer.text: A calculation is a beginning, not a declaration that everything is correct. Check the proposal during easy rides and build experience with your own bike. Ask for help if the position remains uncertain or symptoms develop. A longer riding goal makes addressing problems early especially worthwhile, rather than something to postpone.

h1: Bike fit for a short torso
rows.quick: Quick answerWith a short torso, the handlebar can feel uncomfortably far away even when saddle height is workable. That does not prove the frame is too large. Check your seated position and brake access first, then compare hand distance without simply moving the saddle forwards to bring your hands closer.
rows.article: The problem: a short torso and distant handlebars You can reach the pedals comfortably, yet the brake hoods always seem just beyond a comfortable distance. You notice yourself sliding forwards or riding with rigid arms. Holding the top of the handlebar may feel easier. Once you return to the hoods, the search for a comfortable position begins again. This may become noticeable on longer stretches spent in the same hand position. Perhaps you have relatively long legs and a short torso, or suspect that because ordinary sizing charts seem unhelpful. A label does not identify the setup that works for you. Arm length, handlebar shape and the current installation also matter. The aim is not to place you in a category. You want to pedal and brake without continually finding another place to sit. This guide helps establish which distance you actually want to change. That prevents a saddle adjustment from hiding a handlebar problem while creating a new difficulty somewhere else. Background: hand distance involves more than frame size The distance you feel runs from where you sit to where your hands actually rest. That complete distance is not given by one frame measurement. Frame, stem, handlebar shape and hood position contribute together. Handlebar height belongs in the comparison too, because you do not reach towards your hands only in a horizontal direction. Frame reach is a geometric measurement referenced to the bottom bracket. It is not the distance from your saddle to your brake hoods. Use such measurements to compare frames, but do not confuse them with the complete position on an assembled bike. The Trek geometry table lists frame reach and stack separately. That distinction also helps when comparing two bikes carrying the same size label. Moving the saddle forwards shortens the distance to the handlebar but also moves your seated position relative to the pedals. It is therefore not a neutral solution to distant handlebars. A workable saddle position deserves its own assessment while pedalling. After that, you can investigate how the position of your hands fits that seated position. A short torso does not predict one required stem length either. Your arms, chosen hand position and intended riding remain relevant. A photograph or body measurement cannot complete that assessment. Pain or tingling does not prove the stem is responsible. An online calculation can make differences visible. A fitter can assess what happens while you pedal and change hand position. Ask for installation advice before moving components that affect brake operation, cables or handlebar attachment. How to approach it with bike fitting Describe where the distance feels excessive: Record whether it happens on the hoods, handlebar tops or drops. Also note whether you slide forwards and when this starts. Compare more than the sensation in your arms alone. Check whether you can brake directly and safely from your usual seated position without having to move your hands first. Separate saddle checks from handlebar checks: Record your current saddle height and seated position with a tape measure and side photograph. Measure in millimetres from fixed reference points. Note where on the saddle you normally sit. Use the bike fit calculator for an initial body-measurement comparison, but do not automatically slide the saddle forwards when hand distance differs considerably. Measure the actual hand position: With the bike upright, measure from a fixed saddle point to your usual supporting hand position. Record the height difference too and take a photograph showing both reference points. This measurement helps track your own adjustments. It is not a universal target that you need to share with any other particular rider. Choose a targeted handlebar change with help: Discuss whether bar height, stem, handlebar shape or hood position is the relevant variable. Change only one of those during the same comparison. Record the original and new measurement and the direction of the change. There is no fixed millimetre step for every short torso. Respect manufacturer limits and leave unfamiliar installation work to a professional. Test braking before the longer comparison: In a safe place, check that you can reach the brakes and steer properly. Then compare two to three easy rides while you remain symptom-free. Use the same hand positions and a similar route. Watch for sliding, tense arms and new pressure on hands or saddle. Return to the recorded safe position if things worsen. Stop when the comparison becomes unsafe: Do not continue with lost sensation or symptoms that affect brake operation. Seek medical assessment for radiating tingling, pain at rest or at night, or swelling. If pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, consult a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. A label describing body proportions is never a substitute for investigating persistent symptoms. Further reading Bike fit and body proportions helps you use body measurements without assigning one compulsory position or component dimension to them. Bike frame size shows which fixed frame measurements to compare when adjustable components do not provide enough room. Bike fit for beginners offers a calm sequence when adjusting and testing a bike still feels unfamiliar. Handlebar width and hood position examines where your hands rest and how you operate the brakes. The bike fit calculator helps organise your own measurements before discussing a different handlebar position. Frequently asked questions How can I be certain that my torso is short? You do not need certainty about that label for an initial check. Record where the position feels uncomfortable and repeat measurements using the same instructions. The aim is useful information about your bike, not a threshold for a body category. A fitter can assess those proportions alongside how you actually move. Does a short torso always mean choosing a smaller frame? No. A different frame changes more than the forward distance. Compare handlebar height, saddle adjustment range and room to mount and dismount safely too. When uncertain, have two complete setups assessed. The smaller size label alone cannot tell you whether the bike will allow a genuinely better riding position. Can I simply sit closer to the hoods before changing anything? You can observe when you move, but avoid making sliding your permanent solution. It also changes where you sit relative to the pedals. First check whether the saddle position is workable. Then discuss how the hoods can become reachable from that position without continually searching further forwards on the saddle. Is replacing the stem always the cheapest solution? You cannot establish that from body proportions alone. The question may concern handlebar height or where the hands rest. First establish which measurement needs to change and whether the installation permits it. rows.article: The problem: knee pain when cycling Your knee feels uncomfortable while pedalling. Perhaps it starts on a climb, after a longer ride or since changing shoes. It cannot identify which tissue is sensitive. You do not need to tolerate pain to prove that a new position works. Record what happens and stop the comparison when symptoms appear. A higher saddle increases the distance you need to reach near the bottom. A lower saddle reduces that distance. That alone does not tell you which position suits you. Your foot is another contact point. A different sole, pedal or cleat can change the relationship between your foot and bike. Comparing saddle height alone may therefore miss an important difference. Record which shoes and pedals you used with that measurement. A familiar rule immediately links pain at the front to a low saddle. That association is not a reliable personal diagnosis. A fitter can assess your cycling position but cannot replace medical assessment. A stationary photograph shows only one moment. It cannot show how much riding load your knee can tolerate. A calculator cannot diagnose the problem either. Use its output as a measurement reference and discuss large differences before adopting them. rows.quick: Quick answerCleat position starts with a shoe that fits and a secure connection to your pedal. If your foot feels forced or your heel touches the crank, inspect the existing installation and record your starting point. Then change only one direction at a time; one fixed position does not suit every rider.
rows.article: The problem: finding your cleat position You clip in and notice that your foot does not feel comfortable on the pedal. Perhaps your heel wants to move outward. Or you feel pressure under the forefoot when pedalling firmly. New shoes can make the same bicycle feel different, even when the cleats match the old markings. That makes adjustment confusing. One friend recommends straight feet, while another pushes every cleat fully backward. Meanwhile, you cannot tell whether the shoe pinches, the cleat needs attention or your ride was harder than usual. Start by noting when the difference appears. Does it happen immediately after clipping in, only uphill or later in the ride? Is it on the left, right or both sides? Record whether you can release safely as well. A fit is not a competition for visual symmetry. You need a repeatable position to assess, without consciously forcing your feet into an uncomfortable direction. Background: position, rotation and movement allowance A cleat connects the shoe to the pedal. Moving it forward or backward changes where that connection sits beneath the foot. Moving it sideways changes where the shoe sits relative to the pedal. Rotating it changes the direction in which the shoe engages. These are separate choices that need separate records. The available rotational movement while riding is often called float. This differs from rotating the cleat beneath the shoe. Release force is another setting again. Extra movement or lower spring tension does not automatically explain a painful foot. Shimano's SPD-SL installation instructions emphasise checking engagement and release and using the specified tightening torque. Always follow the instructions for your exact system. A value or component for another pedal is not a safe substitute. Also consider the shoe's fit. If your foot moves inside it, the relationship between foot and cleat can change as you pedal. Tightening the closure may add discomfort without fixing the original fit. New shoes therefore need a fresh assessment rather than simply copied markings. An online assessment can help organise the starting information. It cannot see how much movement your foot seeks under load. A photograph of your knees cannot determine the ideal cleat angle either. When uncertain, a fitter can inspect movement and equipment together. A clinician can assess symptoms that also occur away from cycling. How to approach it with bike fitting Start with equipment and symptoms. Check the model names of your shoes, pedals and cleats. Find the relevant manual. Look for loose bolts, damage and wear. Do not test a cleat that shifts or releases unpredictably. Ask a mechanic to restore correct installation if you cannot assess its safety. Record the original position. Take a photograph directly beneath each sole. Mark the outline with a removable pen that will not damage the material. Record positions against markings in millimetres. Include shoe size, insole and socks. This lets you return to the starting setup without relying on memory. Choose one specific question. Are you investigating foot direction, space beside the crank or position under the forefoot? Do not change rotation and fore-aft position together. Record displacement in millimetres, or an angle in degrees when your measuring tool can reliably show it. No universal adjustment increment fits every system and symptom. Respect installation limits. Make only a change permitted by the manual. Use suitable tools and the tightening torque for your combination. Let a fitter help choose the first direction when there is no clear reason for a change. An arbitrary correction based on knee pain can introduce a second problem. Check away from traffic first. Practise clipping in and releasing with secure support. Test each foot separately and check clearance beside the crank. Ride only when this works reliably. Then compare two to three easy rides per change, provided no symptoms develop. Keep the route, shoes and other settings as similar as possible. Assess and return when needed. Record comfort, release and any new symptoms. Stop if things worsen and restore the marked position with correct installation. The bike fit calculator helps review your overall position, but does not calculate a personal cleat angle. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, seek a fitter and medical advice where appropriate. Do not wait through all the test rides when warning signs appear. Check fit, installation and release again before assessing the new combination during a normal ride. Is more rotational freedom always more comfortable? More room is not automatically better. rows.article: The problem: which bike frame size really fits? You are looking for a bike and fall exactly between two sizes in the chart. One seller describes the smaller size as sporty, while another calls the larger size comfortable. A used bike looks appealing, but its size number differs from your current bike. A straightforward buying question quickly becomes a collection of conflicting rules of thumb. Perhaps you already own a bike and wonder whether its size is wrong. The handlebar feels far away or you cannot put the saddle where you want it. That can justify checking the available adjustment range, but it does not independently prove the frame size is incorrect. This guide helps separate the fixed shape of a frame from the parts that remain adjustable. You are not seeking the right label, but a bike that allows a workable riding position. Write down which measurements and actions matter to you before choosing between two offers. Background: a size label does not describe the complete bike A frame has fixed dimensions. The assembled bike adds a seatpost, saddle, stem and handlebar, among other parts. Together they determine where the contact points can sit. A suitable frame therefore still needs an individual setup. Conversely, adjustable parts cannot compensate for every difference in frame shape without limits. Stack and reach help describe that fixed shape. Stack is the vertical distance from the bottom bracket to the top of the head tube. Reach describes the horizontal distance between those references. The Trek geometry table shows those directions separately. Always compare such values for the actual model and model year you are considering. These dimensions are not saddle height or distance to the hoods. Stem, handlebar shape and saddle position belong in that second comparison. Clearance above the top tube also tells only one part of the story. You need to mount and dismount safely and operate the bike while seated. Your height helps create an initial shortlist. Inseam adds information about the relationship between your legs and the rest of your body. Neither alone tells you how the complete position feels. Include your normal shoes and intended riding in the comparison. An online size proposal helps you ask focused questions. It does not approve a used bike or its installation. Ask a mechanic about uncertain technical adjustment room. A fitter can help when two complete setups seem possible but feel different. Pain also requires a separate assessment; a size label is not a diagnosis. How to approach it with bike fitting Measure before comparing models: Measure height and inseam following the instructions in the frame size calculator. Use a tape measure and ask someone to help with readings. Repeat the measurement if your position or reference point was unclear. Record the units and method so a second calculation does not quietly depend on different inputs from the first. Record the exact bike details: Find the model, year and size in the manufacturer's geometry information. Do not compare only a letter or number across brands. Place stack, reach and relevant adjustment limits alongside one another. If reliable information is missing for a used bike, ask for an inspection rather than treating the advertisement as a measurement report. Identify the desired contact points: Use a comfortable existing bike as a reference if you have one. Measure saddle height and handlebar position from consistent points and record the dimensions in millimetres. Without such a reference, use the calculated proposal as an initial question. Have someone check whether the candidate bike can approach that position within manufacturer limits. Assess the complete setup: Check mounting, dismounting, seated pedalling and access to the brakes. Compare bikes with saddle and hand positions made as similar as possible, not with arbitrary shop setups. Do not exceed installation limits to make a size appear suitable. Ask a professional before moving a seatpost, stem or handlebar that you cannot safely adjust yourself. Separate a test ride from a final verdict: A short test ride does not cover every situation in your normal riding. Record what you could check and discuss what remains uncertain before buying. On your own bike, test one safe adjustment over two to three easy rides while you remain symptom-free. Preserve the original measurements and return to the recorded safe position if things become worse. Set a limit on further adjustments: Stop if you cannot brake, steer or dismount safely. Do not try to rescue an unusable setup through repeated component changes without professional assessment. Seek medical help for lost sensation, radiating tingling, pain at rest or at night, or swelling. If pain persists after three to four careful adjustments, involve a fitter and, where appropriate, a clinician. Further reading Bike fit and body proportions helps use your own proportions without treating a size label as a complete description of your position. Bike fit for a short torso investigates distant handlebars before concluding that a smaller frame is required. Bike fit for beginners gives a safe sequence for the first checks on a new or borrowed bike. Saddle height helps record one contact point before comparing the adjustment room on different bikes. The frame size calculator provides an initial selection based on your own measurements and chosen bike type. Frequently asked questions Should I always choose the smaller of two possible sizes? No. Compare the complete position each bike can provide. A smaller size can also change the available handlebar height, so examine more than the forward distance. Ask for a test setup with similar contact points and record where each bike reaches its installation limits before deciding which is more suitable for you. Can the same size number feel different with another brand? Yes. Do not treat the number as a complete geometry description. Check the exact model, size table and fitted components. Even with similar fixed frame dimensions, handlebar and saddle positions may differ. Measure those contact points separately when you are trying to transfer a comfortable position from your current bike to another one. Is clearance above the top tube enough to assess the size? No. It is one check alongside saddle adjustment, handlebar position and brake operation. A bike can provide enough standing clearance yet still feel uncomfortable while riding. Also assess how you mount, dismount and reach the brakes safely from your normal seated position rather than relying on one stationary comparison alone. Can a different stem always correct an unsuitable size? No. A stem changes part of the position, not every fixed frame dimension. rows.description: Unsure about road handlebar width? Learn to assess width and hood position separately, measure your setup and compare safely before buying new parts.

rows.quick: Quick answerHandlebar width involves more than your shoulders: the position and shape of the brake hoods matter too. Start by measuring where your hands actually rest and checking relaxed steering and braking. Do not immediately buy a narrower bar; a different hood position or reach needs to be assessed separately first.
rows.article: The problem: handlebar width Your hands sit further apart than feels comfortable. Or your wrists bend awkwardly when you hold the brake hoods. Perhaps the bar tops feel fine, but the drops seem difficult to reach while braking. A different handlebar width may look like the obvious solution. Yet the number printed on the bar does not describe every hand position. A bar may be wider at the bottom than at the hoods. The hoods themselves also occupy space and change the supporting surface. You may only notice the difference after a longer ride. Your shoulders rise, your arms feel tense or you keep looking for another position. Record where that happens and whether braking still feels easy. This guide helps separate width, hood position and reach. It does not choose an exact bar size from one body measurement. Start with your existing handlebar and observe without loosening parts. Pain or numbness is not a reason to keep riding for a more complete test. Background: width is more than the number on the bar A handlebar has several dimensions. Width describes the distance between two reference points, but manufacturers may use different points. Check where the manufacturer measures. Do not compare an outside measurement with a centre-to-centre measurement as if they were identical. Brake hood position changes where your hands rest. On a bar with flared drops, the lower hand positions sit further apart. A single width number therefore cannot describe the space you experience on the hoods. Measure both positions if you feel a clear difference between holding the hoods and the drops. Reach and drop matter as well. The curve of the bar can place your hands further forward or lower. A narrower bar therefore does not automatically solve excessive reach. Your support on the saddle also affects how much you lean on your hands. Distinguish the position of the whole hood from the reach to the brake lever. Some models allow the lever distance to be adjusted separately. The Shimano user manual for operation and adjustment directs users to a dealer for adjustments not described there. Always use information for your own model, rather than copying an unfamiliar screw adjustment from a video. Shoulder width can support a discussion about sizes, but it is not an automatic ordering specification. A photograph also cannot show your confidence while braking or steering. An online bike fit can organise your starting information, but cannot independently choose a safe, comfortable handlebar shape. How to approach it with bike fitting Record your current handlebar: Note the brand, model and stated width. Check the product specification to see where that dimension is measured. Use a tape to measure between matching points at both brake hoods. Repeat this at the drops and record both distances in millimetres. Take photographs from the front and side. Check your hands without adjusting anything: Stabilise the bicycle with help from another person. Hold the hoods and then the drops as you would while riding. Observe your wrists, shoulders and access to the brake levers. You must be able to reach the controls without an insecure grip. Compare left and right, but do not force artificial symmetry. Separate width from distance: Record whether your hands feel too far apart or too far forward. Those are different questions. Use the bike fit calculator to organise your body measurements and position, not to prescribe handlebar width. Discuss with a fitter whether bar shape, hood position, lever reach or overall reach deserves attention first. Choose one safe comparison: No universal number of millimetres or degrees improves every brake hood position. Record an agreed change against your photographs and measurements. Use only adjustments permitted by the component instructions. After installation, check security and brake operation. Have a mechanic do the work if you are unsure which bolt or adjuster is involved. A different handlebar width may also affect cables and hoses; have these checked in advance. Compare the result calmly: Begin in a safe place with steering and braking checks before planning a normal ride. Then compare two to three easy rides, only while you remain symptom-free. Keep gloves, route and effort as consistent as possible. Assess both the hoods and the drops. Restore the safely recorded original position and seek advice if the result is worse. Take warning signs seriously: Stop for pain, tingling, numbness or uncertain access to the brakes. Seek medical assessment for persistent changes in sensation, weakness, swelling, pain at rest or at night, and radiating symptoms. Have recurring tingling assessed too, as recommended by the NHS advice on pins and needles. If symptoms remain after three to four careful adjustments, involve a fitter and a clinician where appropriate. Do not wait through that sequence with sensory loss or braking problems; safety matters more than completing a comparison. Further reading Bike fit for a short torso helps distinguish forward reach from the distance between your hands. Bike frame size explains why a suitable handlebar position also requires room for adjustment on the bicycle. Bike fit for beginners offers a calm sequence of checks before you replace components. Cycling power and pacing helps you keep riding effort consistent during comparison rides. The bike fit calculator organises body measurements and your preferred position, but does not prescribe an exact handlebar width. Frequently asked questions Does a narrower handlebar make me faster? Do not choose a bar solely on a general speed claim. You still need safe braking, steering and access to different hand positions. This guide does not calculate aerodynamic gains. Compare comfort and control first; a position you cannot hold comfortably is not an automatic improvement for your own rides. Should my brake hoods point straight forward? There is no universal angle for every bar, hood and rider. Components must still remain within their installation instructions. Have hand position and access to the controls assessed together. Do not turn the hoods far inward simply because another rider does; their equipment and circumstances may differ from yours. Can I move the brake lever closer to my fingers? Some models offer separate reach adjustment. Check the instructions for your exact model or ask a mechanic. Rotating the entire hood is not the same as changing lever reach. After any permitted adjustment, check that you can maintain a secure grip and that the brakes operate normally and safely. Which details help when choosing another handlebar? Keep the brand, model, width measurement method, distances at the hoods and drops, and photographs from both angles. Record which hand position feels comfortable and where using the controls is difficult. Bring your usual gloves to an assessment. That lets you compare actual contact points rather than product names alone.Organise your measurements and riding position before comparing a different handlebar setup with a fitter.Calculate your bike fit

sections.title: How to approach it with bike fitting
sections.text: Record your current handlebar: Note the brand, model and stated width. Check the product specification to see where that dimension is measured. Use a tape to measure between matching points at both brake hoods. Repeat this at the drops and record both distances in millimetres. Take photographs from the front and side. Check your hands without adjusting anything: Stabilise the bicycle with help from another person. Hold the hoods and then the drops as you would while riding. Observe your wrists, shoulders and access to the brake levers. You must be able to reach the controls without an insecure grip. Compare left and right, but do not force artificial symmetry. Separate width from distance: Record whether your hands feel too far apart or too far forward. Those are different questions. Use the bike fit calculator to organise your body measurements and position, not to prescribe handlebar width. Discuss with a fitter whether bar shape, hood position, lever reach or overall reach deserves attention first. Choose one safe comparison: No universal number of millimetres or degrees improves every brake hood position. Record an agreed change against your photographs and measurements. Use only adjustments permitted by the component instructions. After installation, check security and brake operation. Have a mechanic do the work if you are unsure which bolt or adjuster is involved. A different handlebar width may also affect cables and hoses; have these checked in advance. Compare the result calmly: Begin in a safe place with steering and braking checks before planning a normal ride. Then compare two to three easy rides, only while you remain symptom-free. Keep gloves, route and effort as consistent as possible. Assess both the hoods and the drops. Restore the safely recorded original position and seek advice if the result is worse. Take warning signs seriously: Stop for pain, tingling, numbness or uncertain access to the brakes. Seek medical assessment for persistent changes in sensation, weakness, swelling, pain at rest or at night, and radiating symptoms. Have recurring tingling assessed too, as recommended by the NHS advice on pins and needles. If symptoms remain after three to four careful adjustments, involve a fitter and a clinician where appropriate. Do not wait through that sequence with sensory loss or braking problems; safety matters more than completing a comparison.

rows.quick: Quick answerCycling shoe insoles should not confuse greater support with greater pressure. Another insole changes contact beneath your foot and the space inside the shoe. rows.article: The problem: assessing cycling shoe insoles You feel a firm edge beneath your arch after installing another insole. Or your foot feels better supported, but the shoe now pinches on top. Perhaps you expect extra support to resolve burning toes. It becomes tempting to keep trying higher or softer insoles. First ask exactly what you want to change. Are you replacing a worn insole, addressing movement inside the shoe or seeking help with recurring discomfort? These situations may need different approaches. The word orthotic does not itself explain what a particular product is suitable for. Describe where you feel the insole and when that begins. Is it different while standing, sitting or only while pedalling? Record the shoe, socks and original insole. Compare both feet without assuming they respond identically. An insole should make your assessment clearer. It is not a reason to accept pressure or numbness as an essential part of getting used to equipment. Background: support within limited space The insole sits between your foot and the shoe's fixed sole. It influences where contact occurs and how much space remains inside the shoe. Height beneath the arch is only one property. Shape, thickness at the forefoot and the fit around the heel matter too. A raised area that feels comfortable beneath one foot may press in an uncomfortable place beneath another. Choosing the highest support is therefore not a universal fitting rule. A high arch in a photograph does not prove which support is needed while cycling either. Shimano describes insoles with interchangeable arch support as part of certain shoes. This shows that support can vary between systems. It does not establish that every rider needs extra height or that such an insole treats a specific symptom. Notice what happens above the foot as well. A different thickness can reduce room at the instep. Tightening the closure to prevent movement may then add pressure. Assess the combination of foot, insole and shoe rather than the loose insole on a table. An insole, a wedge and a spacer beneath the cleat are different interventions. They do not change the same parts of the connection to the bicycle. Do not combine them on your own to correct a feeling of asymmetry. Online measurements can organise your observations, but cannot prescribe a medical orthotic. If you already use prescribed insoles, discuss changes with your clinician. A fitter can assess the cycling environment without replacing that medical assessment. How to approach it with bike fitting Record the existing setup. Remove the original insole and photograph its upper and lower surfaces. Note the brand, version and any separate support elements. Check that it lies flat inside the shoe rather than curling. A shifted or damaged insole needs attention before you experiment with more support. Check the shoe with your usual socks. Look for pressure around the forefoot, instep and heel. Separate insufficient room from a local edge beneath the foot. Measure both feet using the shoe manufacturer's instructions and record millimetres. No foot-width measurement alone tells you how much arch support to add. Choose a suitable replacement system. Check its size, shape and compatibility with the shoe. Follow instructions for any interchangeable elements. Do not casually stack two complete insoles. Trim or heat them only when the manufacturer gives clear instructions. Have prescribed insoles assessed by your clinician before altering them yourself. Make one comparison. Keep shoes, socks, cleat position and saddle settings unchanged. Compare the original insole with one suitable alternative. Describe where contact feels different, rather than only whether it feels softer. Do not choose additional height because another cyclist uses it. There is no universal millimetre increment for supporting every arch. Test briefly and gently. First check that the shoe closes without pinching and that you can release safely. Then compare two to three easy rides per change while remaining symptom-free. Record the location and timing of discomfort. If the foot becomes painful or numb, stop and restore the previous comfortable combination. Review overall position separately. The bike fit calculator provides a starting point for general bicycle measurements. It does not prescribe insoles or assess a foot condition. Do not use its result to justify adding a lift or wedge beneath one foot. Bring your notes to a fitter when the cause remains unclear. Warning signs: stop for loss of sensation, spreading tingling or weakness. Have swelling and pain at rest or at night medically assessed. If symptoms remain after three to four careful adjustments, seek a fitter and medical advice where appropriate. Discuss existing medical foot problems earlier; repeated equipment trials are not a substitute for care. rows.description: Unsure about your pace? Learn how power, FTP and effort work together, choose an easy reference ride and compare your position without pushing harder.

rows.quick: Quick answerCycling power and pacing belong together, but a number on your bike computer cannot explain everything. Begin with an easy ride where your position and effort feel sustainable. Treat FTP as an estimated reference, not an instruction to ride hard every day. Only then compare the effect of a setup change.
rows.article: The problem: cycling power and pacing You start with a clear power target. Yet the same number feels progressively harder during the ride. You slide along the saddle or lift your shoulders. Afterwards, you cannot tell whether you rode too hard or sat in an unsuitable position. Perhaps you ride without a power meter. Your friend's speed seems manageable until the wind changes. You try to stay alongside and your hands become uncomfortable. Changing the handlebars then seems an obvious solution. Both situations make comparison difficult. You alter not only load, but often your posture and attention too. Fatigue on a demanding ride reveals little about a small setup change. This guide helps separate those questions. First identify the measurement you are using and how the ride felt. Then choose a controlled, easy comparison. You do not need to set a new personal record to learn something useful. Background: what the numbers can explain Power describes mechanical work delivered per unit of time. Speed describes how quickly you move forward. The two are not interchangeable. Wind, gradient, surface and aerodynamic resistance affect speed at the same effort. Lower speed therefore does not automatically mean a worse outcome. FTP is a practical reference for planning effort. Its estimate depends on the test or calculation used. An older value may no longer reflect your current fitness. Record when you established it and which method you used. The FTP and W/kg calculator uses the information you enter. W/kg divides power by body mass. That makes two values comparable, but does not describe your complete performance. Nor does the number establish whether your riding position is suitable. A relaxed test position helps make a comparison useful. Riding hard uphill on one outing and gently on flat roads on another means comparing different conditions. Heat, recovery and food can also influence how the ride feels. Record those differences instead of attributing everything to a millimetre of adjustment. An online calculation cannot observe how you move when tired. It cannot establish why your back or knee hurts. That distinction needs your description, a safe comparison and sometimes an assessment. Use the numbers to focus your observations rather than to dismiss symptoms or pressure yourself into completing an unsuitable ride. How to approach it with bike fitting Record your reference. Note the date, your current FTP and the method used to establish it. Label an estimate clearly as an estimate. Use the same measurement source for later comparisons, provided it is working correctly. Without a power meter, describe your effort and whether you can talk comfortably. Do not invent a wattage merely to fill an input field. Choose one easy reference ride. Use a familiar route without a performance target. Start at an effort that lets you maintain a relaxed position. Record when you lean more heavily on your hands, slide on the saddle or change your pedalling. Record wind and surface too. Stop for pain or reduced sensation; a complete activity file never matters more than your symptoms. Separate effort from setup. If the first ride was too hard, reduce the load before adjusting components. Leave saddle and handlebars unchanged for now. This helps establish whether the same discomfort also occurs on an easy ride. Do not assess a new position immediately with a maximal test. You would not know which part of the experience came from fatigue. Choose one measurable setup question. This might concern reach to the hoods or a saddle that feels different while pedalling. Measure the current position in millimetres using fixed reference points. Take a photograph before changing anything. Then follow the guide for that component. This power guide gives no universal saddle correction: a power value cannot establish the appropriate adjustment direction. Compare two to three easy rides. Keep route, equipment and intended effort as consistent as possible. Change one component at a time. Record comfort, control and symptoms after each ride, rather than average speed alone. If things worsen, stop the comparison. Return to your recorded baseline only if it was safe. Discuss uncertainty with a fitter before continuing. Recognise warning signs. Pain at rest or at night, swelling and radiating tingling need medical assessment. Do not wait until the test sequence ends when sensation is reduced. Seek support if position-related pain persists after three to four careful adjustments. Higher power does not prove that continuing is sensible. Improving fitness and an unresolved contact-point problem can exist at the same time. Further reading Bike fit for beginners helps you record a relaxed baseline position before comparing performance with previous rides. Bike fit and body proportions explains why a stronger friend's riding position does not automatically suit your own proportions. What is cycling FTP? explains this training reference and why the testing method belongs alongside the number. Cycling power and speed: what changes? explains why the same effort produces different speeds as riding conditions change. Cycling climb time: plan your effort helps you use an estimated climbing duration without turning it into a compulsory race pace. Use the FTP and W/kg calculator to compare your own inputs without forcing another maximal effort simply to obtain a number. Frequently asked questions Should I retest FTP after a bike fit? Not to assess a small adjustment. Begin with easy rides and check comfort and control. A maximal test introduces fatigue into the comparison. Perhaps you ride without a power meter. Your friend's speed seems manageable until the wind changes. You try to stay alongside and your hands become uncomfortable. Changing the handlebars then seems an obvious solution.
Both situations make comparison difficult. You alter not only load, but often your posture and attention too. Fatigue on a demanding ride reveals little about a small setup change.

This guide helps separate those questions. First identify the measurement you are using and how the ride felt. Then choose a controlled, easy comparison. You do not need to set a new personal record to learn something useful.
Power describes mechanical work delivered per unit of time. Speed describes how quickly you move forward. The two are not interchangeable.
Wind, gradient, surface and aerodynamic resistance affect speed at the same effort. Lower speed therefore does not automatically mean a worse outcome.

FTP is a practical reference for planning effort. Its estimate depends on the test or calculation used. An older value may no longer reflect your current fitness. Record when you established it and which method you used.

The FTP and W/kg calculator uses the information you enter. W/kg divides power by body mass. That makes two values comparable, but does not describe your complete performance. Nor does the number establish whether your riding position is suitable.

A relaxed test position helps make a comparison useful. Riding hard uphill on one outing and gently on flat roads on another means comparing different conditions. Heat, recovery and food can also influence how the ride feels. Record those differences instead of attributing everything to a millimetre of adjustment.

An online calculation cannot observe how you move when tired. It cannot establish why your back or knee hurts. That distinction needs your description, a safe comparison and sometimes an assessment. Use the numbers to focus your observations rather than to dismiss symptoms or pressure yourself into completing an unsuitable ride.

Do not assess a new position immediately with a maximal test. You would not know which part of the experience came from fatigue.

Choose one measurable setup question. This might concern reach to the hoods or a saddle that feels different while pedalling. Measure the current position in millimetres using fixed reference points. Take a photograph before changing anything.
Then follow the guide for that component. This power guide gives no universal saddle correction: a power value cannot establish the appropriate adjustment direction.

sections.text: Crankset width and the distance between your feet are not the same measurement. Crankset Q-factor describes the distance between the pedal mounting faces. Pedal axles then place the pedals farther outward. Cleat position additionally determines where the shoes sit relative to those pedals. TIME describes the relationship between crank width, pedal axles and stance width. Always check the reference points used by a manufacturer. A measurement for one pedal axle is not directly comparable with the total distance between both feet. Moving a cleat toward the inner side of the sole places the shoe farther outward once clipped in. This differs from rotating the cleat. With rotation, the heel may be the part that needs more room. Check which direction you are actually changing. Washers and longer axles are not universal solutions. Additional spacing at the connection changes installation. The required thread engagement and any clearance for a power meter remain safety considerations. Use only components and installation methods approved for your pedal and crank. Wahoo provides specific installation requirements for SPEEDPLAY POWER, including clearance around the power meter. Those instructions do not authorise using the same washers with other pedals. An online tool can organise this equipment information, but cannot choose a personal stance width from your height. With pain or uncertainty about movement, a fitter is more useful than guessing with extra components.

sections.title: How to approach it with bike fitting
sections.text: List the equipment without loosening anything. Record the crank model, pedal model, axle version, shoes and cleats. Photograph both connections. Find current manuals for the exact combination. An already installed washer does not prove that installation is correct or that another washer can be added safely. Record clear reference points. Note manufacturer dimensions in millimetres and specify what each describes. Photograph cleat placement beneath both soles. Do not measure diagonally between shoes and call that crank width. Ask a mechanic to inspect installation if components or measurement points remain unclear. Choose the relevant direction. When space beside the crank is limited, first distinguish shoe position from heel direction. Check whether it happens with only one pair of shoes. Do not change cleats, saddle and pedals simultaneously. Discuss knee pain separately; its location does not automatically tell you that a wider stance is needed. Stay within approved limits. A sideways cleat adjustment must remain within the mounting range. Record displacement in millimetres and keep rotation unchanged when comparing width alone. For other axles, washers or extenders, obtain confirmation from the manufacturer or mechanic. There is no universal permitted washer thickness for every pedal. Check safety before the test ride. Have tightening torque, attachment and clearance checked against the manuals. Practise engagement and release with support. Pay attention to the heel while releasing as well. Do not test a questionable threaded connection to discover whether wider feels better; safe installation comes before the fit experiment. Compare and record the result. Complete two to three easy rides with one change, provided you remain symptom-free. Record crank contact, comfort and new symptoms. Stop if things worsen and restore the previous safe setup. Consult a clinician for swelling and pain at rest or at night. If pain remains after three to four careful adjustments, seek a fitter and medical advice where appropriate. Technically unsafe installation needs immediate correction, not another test ride.

rows.quick: Snel antwoordEen fiets afstellen voor beginners begint met controle, niet met een lage wedstrijdhouding. Een onbekende of oude afstelling kan slecht aansluiten op hoe je nu fietst. rows.article: Het probleem: fiets afstellen voor beginners Je hebt een nieuwe fiets, leent er een of haalt je oude fiets weer uit de schuur. De eerste kilometers voelen onwennig. Je schuift op het zadel, zoekt steeds een andere handpositie of houdt je armen gespannen. Misschien ging een korte proefrit prima, maar voelt dezelfde houding tijdens een langere rit minder prettig. Dat maakt beginnen verwarrend. Je weet nog niet wat gewone inspanning is en wat bij de afstelling hoort. Ook een terugkerende fietser kan twijfelen. De stand van vroeger voelt niet automatisch prettig na een lange onderbreking. Je hoeft niet meteen onderdelen te vervangen of de houding van een ervaren fietser over te nemen. Begin met de vraag of je ontspannen kunt trappen, vooruitkijken, sturen en remmen. Deze gids helpt je die eerste controle ordenen. Pijn, tintelingen en gevoelsverlies zijn geen verplichte gewenningsfase. Noteer wanneer iets begint, zodat je niet op basis van een losse indruk alles tegelijk verandert. Achtergrond: wennen is niet hetzelfde als passend zitten Je zitpositie ontstaat tussen zadel, pedalen en stuur. Een verandering aan het zadel verandert dus meer dan alleen de hoogte. Ook de afstand tot je handen kan anders aanvoelen. Daarom is één ongemakkelijk contactpunt niet meteen bewijs voor één verkeerde maat. Een geleende fiets staat nog ingesteld voor iemand anders. Bij een eigen oude fiets kunnen kleding, schoenen en gebruik veranderd zijn. Misschien maak je nu rustige tochten in plaats van snelle groepsritten. Begin bij dat huidige doel, niet bij een vroegere foto. De framemaat begrenst wat je kunt aanpassen. Onderdelen hebben bovendien hun eigen montagegrenzen. De Trek-gebruikershandleiding waarschuwt bijvoorbeeld dat de zadelpen voldoende in het frame moet blijven. Een markering is geen uitnodiging om daar voorbij te schuiven voor een berekende ideale maat. Ook je rit maakt verschil voor de beoordeling. Een korte, rustige rondgang is een andere vergelijking dan een zware tocht. Als je tegelijk langer rijdt en onderdelen verstelt, weet je minder goed welke verandering bij je ervaring hoort. Houd de eerste vergelijkingen daarom eenvoudig. Je hoeft geen vermogensmeter te hebben om route, duur en gevoel te noteren. Online kun je maten vastleggen en een eerste voorstel berekenen. Zo pak je het aan met bikefitting Maak de fiets eerst veilig: Controleer banden, remmen en vastzittende onderdelen volgens de handleiding. Gebruik geen proefrit om te ontdekken of een los stuur toch blijft zitten. Vraag een fietsenmaker bij twijfel over montage. Controleer ook of je in je normale handpositie de remmen kunt bedienen zonder naar voren te schuiven. Bewaar de beginstand: Zet de fiets recht op een vlakke vloer. Gebruik een meetlint voor de zadelhoogte. Meet vanaf het midden van de trapas naar een vast punt op het zadel. Noteer dat punt en de maat in millimeters. Maak een zijfoto en noteer de stand van zadel en stuur, zodat je later dezelfde uitgangspositie kunt terugvinden. Bereken een eerste vergelijking: Meet je lichaam volgens de instructies van de bikefitcalculator. Controleer de eenheden en herhaal een meting wanneer je twijfelt. Behandel het resultaat als voorstel, niet als verplicht eindpunt. Een groot verschil met je huidige positie vraagt eerst om een controle van de invoer en de meetwijze. Kies één begrijpelijke wijziging: Begin alleen aan een onderdeel dat je veilig kunt afstellen. Noteer de oude en nieuwe maat, inclusief de richting. Er is geen vaste millimeterstap voor iedere beginner en ieder onderdeel. Blijf binnen de fabrikantgrenzen en gebruik het voorgeschreven gereedschap. Laat een onbekende stuur- of zadelconstructie door een vakman aanpassen. Noteer ook nieuwe drukpunten; alleen een prettiger zadelgevoel is niet het hele resultaat. Keer bij verslechtering terug naar de vastgelegde veilige stand. Maak een testreeks niet af ten koste van pijn. Herken de grens van zelf proberen: Stop bij gevoelsverlies, uitstralende tintelingen of klachten die je controle over de fiets verminderen. Bij pijn in rust of 's nachts, zwelling of aanhoudende klachten vraag je medische beoordeling. Blijft pijn na drie tot vier zorgvuldige aanpassingen bestaan, schakel dan een fitter en zo nodig een arts in. Een nieuwe fiets hoort geen reden te zijn om alarmsignalen te negeren. Verder lezen Fiets afstellen op lichaamsbouw legt uit waarom de positie van een even lange vriend geen betrouwbaar persoonlijk startpunt is. Framemaat fiets bepalen helpt je controleren of de fiets genoeg ruimte biedt voor een passende afstelling. Zadelhoogte instellen werkt de eerste zadelmeting uit voordat je aan andere contactpunten begint. Stuurbreedte racefiets en remgrepen helpt je veilig handcontact beoordelen zonder direct een ander stuur te kopen. Vermogen en tempo bij fietsen helpt je inspanning tijdens vergelijkingsritten bewust en overzichtelijk te houden. De bikefitcalculator verzamelt je lichaamsmaten en geeft een eerste voorstel dat je op de fiets kunt beoordelen. Veelgestelde vragen Heb ik meteen speciale fietsschoenen nodig voor mijn eerste afstelling? Nee. Leg vast welke schoenen en pedalen je nu gebruikt en vergelijk daarmee je eerste ritten. Andere schoenen kunnen de uitgangssituatie veranderen. Controleer je positie opnieuw wanneer je overstapt, in plaats van tegelijk schoenen, zadel en stuur te veranderen. Koop niet eerst een compleet nieuwe uitrusting om één onduidelijk ongemak op te lossen. Kan ik mijn oude zadelstand gebruiken wanneer ik opnieuw begin? Je kunt die stand vastleggen als uitgangspunt als de montage veilig is. Hij bewijst niet dat dezelfde houding nog bij je huidige ritten past. Begin rustig en controleer rembereik, trappen en comfort opnieuw. Verander alleen iets wanneer je een duidelijke reden en een veilige manier van vergelijken hebt. Moet ik altijd met beide voeten plat bij de grond kunnen? Gebruik dat niet als enige maat voor je zadelhoogte. De manier van op- en afstappen en het type fiets spelen mee. Vraag begeleiding als stoppen onzeker voelt. Je moet veilig kunnen stoppen en afstappen, maar een zadelmeting beoordeel je ook tijdens het trappen. Is een gratis berekening genoeg voordat ik langere tochten maak? Een berekening is een begin, geen verklaring dat alles goed staat. Controleer de uitkomst tijdens rustige ritten en bouw ervaring op met je eigen fiets. Vraag hulp als je houding onzeker blijft of klachten ontstaan. sections.text: Begin met een klachtenoverzicht: Noteer welke knie en welke plek gevoelig zijn. Schrijf de activiteit, het beginmoment en recente veranderingen op. Vermeld ook pijn bij lopen, rust of slapen. Stop met de rit wanneer pijn ontstaat; een test is geen opdracht om de klacht op te wekken. Bewaar je uitgangspositie: Zet de fiets recht en maak een duidelijke zijfoto. Meet met een meetlint vanaf het midden van de trapas tot hetzelfde punt bovenop het zadel. Noteer die afstand in millimeters, samen met je schoenen, pedalen en de stand van de zadelrails. Markeer de oude zadelpenpositie met verwijderbare tape zonder veiligheidsmarkeringen af te dekken. Controleer wat werkelijk veranderd is: Vergelijk je notities met de vorige prettige afstelling. Denk ook aan schoenzolen, cleats en ritbelasting. Draai niet tegelijk aan zadelhoogte, setback en cleats. Laat een fietsenmaker controleren of onderdelen goed vastzitten wanneer je daarover twijfelt. Gebruik een berekening als gesprekspunt: Vul je gemeten binnenbeenlengte in de zadelhoogtecalculator in. Vergelijk de aanbevolen startpositie met je meting. Een verschil verklaart geen kniepijn en is geen reden voor een grote sprong. Bespreek bij klachten eerst met een fitter welke ene verandering zinvol is. Een vergelijking van bijvoorbeeld 2–3 mm zadelhoogte is klein en omkeerbaar, maar geen behandeling of vaste aanbeveling. Noteer het verschil en herstel bij verslechtering de veilig vastgelegde oude positie. Volg bij montage de onderdelenhandleiding en het aanhaalmoment. Dat zijn verschillende keuzes, die je afzonderlijk moet vastleggen. De beschikbare draaiende bewegingsruimte tijdens het fietsen is de draaivrijheid. Dat is iets anders dan het plaatje draaien onder de schoen. Ook de kracht voor uitklikken is een aparte instelling. Meer bewegingsruimte of minder veerspanning verklaart niet automatisch een pijnlijke voet. De montage-instructie van Shimano voor SPD-SL benadrukt het controleren van in- en uitklikken en het voorgeschreven aanhaalmoment. Gebruik altijd de instructie voor jouw precieze systeem. Een waarde of onderdeel voor een ander pedaal is geen veilige vervanging. Kijk daarnaast naar de pasvorm van de schoen. Als je voet daarin verschuift, verandert de verhouding tussen voet en plaatje tijdens het trappen. Een strakkere sluiting kan ongemak toevoegen zonder de oorspronkelijke pasvorm te herstellen. Nieuwe schoenen vragen daarom een nieuwe controle, niet alleen het overnemen van lijnen. Een online beoordeling kan de uitgangssituatie helpen ordenen. Ze ziet niet hoeveel ruimte je voet zoekt onder belasting. Ook een foto van je knieën bepaalt geen ideale plaatjeshoek. Bij twijfel kan een fitter beweging en materiaal samen bekijken, terwijl een arts klachten beoordeelt die niet alleen bij fietsen optreden.

sections.title: Zo pak je het aan met bikefitting
sections.text: Begin bij materiaal en klachten. Controleer modelnamen van schoenen, pedalen en plaatjes. Zoek de bijbehorende handleiding op. Kijk naar losse bouten, beschadigingen en slijtage. Test niet met een plaatje dat verschuift of onvoorspelbaar loskomt. Laat een fietsenmaker de montage herstellen als je de veiligheid niet kunt beoordelen. Leg de oorspronkelijke stand vast. Maak een foto recht onder iedere zool. Markeer de omtrek met een verwijderbare stift die het materiaal niet aantast. Noteer de positie langs maatstrepen in millimeters. Vermeld schoenmaat, binnenzool en sokken. Zo kun je later teruggaan zonder op je geheugen te vertrouwen. Kies één concrete vraag. Gaat het om de richting van je voet, ruimte naast de crank of plaats onder de voorvoet? Verander niet tegelijk draaiing en lengtepositie. Noteer een verplaatsing in millimeters of een hoek in graden als jouw hulpmiddel die betrouwbaar meet. Er is geen algemene stapgrootte die voor elk systeem en iedere klacht klopt. Blijf binnen de montagegrenzen. Maak alleen een wijziging die de handleiding toestaat. Gebruik geschikt gereedschap en het aanhaalmoment van jouw combinatie. Laat een fitter de eerste richting kiezen wanneer je geen duidelijke aanleiding hebt. Een willekeurige correctie op basis van kniepijn kan een tweede probleem toevoegen. Controleer eerst zonder verkeersdruk. Oefen in- en uitklikken met veilige ondersteuning. Controleer beide voeten afzonderlijk en controleer vrije ruimte langs de crank. Ga pas rijden wanneer dit betrouwbaar werkt. Vergelijk daarna twee tot drie rustige ritten per wijziging, zolang je geen klachten krijgt. Houd route, schoenen en andere instellingen zo gelijk mogelijk. Beoordeel en keer zo nodig terug. Noteer comfort, loskomen en eventuele nieuwe klachten. Stop bij verslechtering en herstel de gemarkeerde stand met correcte montage. De bikefitcalculator helpt je algemene fietspositie bekijken, maar berekent geen persoonlijke schoenplaatjeshoek. Waarschuwingssignalen: stop bij gevoelloosheid, krachtverlies of uitstralende tintelingen. Bespreek zwelling en pijn in rust of 's nachts met een arts. Blijft pijn na drie tot vier zorgvuldige aanpassingen bestaan, vraag een fitter en zo nodig arts om hulp. Wacht bij deze waarschuwingssignalen niet eerst alle testritten af.

sections.text: Je tenen raken de voorkant niet, maar de schoen drukt langs de voorvoet. Of je kiest een ruimere maat en merkt vervolgens dat de hiel beweegt. Soms knelt alleen de bovenkant, terwijl er naast de voet voldoende ruimte lijkt. Dan vertelt het maatnummer maar een deel van het verhaal. Dat merk je niet altijd direct bij het passen. Tijdens een langere rit wil je de sluiting losser zetten. Met dikkere sokken voelt dezelfde schoen anders. Na een wissel van binnenzool kan juist de wreef meer druk krijgen. Schrijf op waar je ruimte mist en waar je voet beweegt. Beoordeel links en rechts apart. Noteer ook welke sokken, binnenzool en sluitingsstand je gebruikt. Daarmee wordt een vergelijking tussen modellen veel duidelijker. Je zoekt niet simpelweg de breedste schoen. Je zoekt een vorm die je voet vasthoudt zonder hem plaatselijk samen te drukken. Die vraag verdient aandacht voordat je schoenplaatjes verplaatst.

sections.title: Achtergrond: lengte, leest en ruimte zijn verschillend
sections.text: De leest is de vorm waarnaar een schoen wordt gemaakt. Twee modellen met hetzelfde maatnummer kunnen daardoor anders aanvoelen. Lengte zegt iets over de ruimte in de lengterichting, maar beschrijft niet automatisch de vorm van de voorvoet, hiel of wreef. Shimano legt bij schoenpasvorm uit dat breedte en schoenvolume naast lengte beoordeeld moeten worden. Een bredere uitvoering kan dus een andere oplossing zijn dan een langere schoen. Dat is een reden om vormen te vergelijken, geen garantie dat één aanduiding bij jouw voet past. Een voetomtrek op papier geeft nuttige informatie, maar geen complete pasvorm. Het papier beschrijft bijvoorbeeld niet hoeveel ruimte je boven de voet nodig hebt. Ook de plaats van naden en sluitingen kan verschillen. Leg daarom naast meetgegevens vast waar je druk daadwerkelijk voelt. Een binnenzool is eveneens onderdeel van de beschikbare ruimte. Wie een dikkere zool toevoegt, verandert niet alleen wat er onder de voet ligt. De voet krijgt ook een andere plek binnen de schoen. Een zool is daarom geen onafhankelijke oplossing voor iedere drukplek. Een schoenplaatje verandert de verbinding met het pedaal, niet de binnenvorm van de schoen. Het is dus onlogisch om eerst plaatjes te draaien als de schoen al knelt voordat je inklikt. Andersom kan goede pasvorm samengaan met een onprettige pedaalpositie. Online kun je maten vergelijken en vragen voorbereiden. Je kunt niet betrouwbaar voelen waar een schoen onder belasting drukt. Een pasafspraak helpt wanneer lengte, breedte en houvast niet tegelijk goed lijken.

sections.title: Zo pak je het aan met bikefitting
sections.text: Beschrijf het probleem voordat je koopt. Noteer de precieze plek: kleine teen, bal van de voet, hiel of wreef. Schrijf op wanneer het begint. Vergelijk met lopen en met andere schoenen. Pijn buiten het fietsen verdient een bredere beoordeling dan alleen een ander fietsmodel of een nieuwe schoenmaat. Meet beide voeten in millimeters. Gebruik papier, een potlood en een liniaal. Volg de meetwijze van het merk waarmee je wilt vergelijken. Noteer voetlengte en de breedste plaats van de voorvoet. Herhaal de meting in dezelfde houding. Een toevallig verschil tussen twee tekeningen is nog geen verschil tussen je voeten. Vergelijk eerst vormen, daarna sluitingen. Neem je gebruikelijke fietssokken en binnenzolen mee naar een pasafspraak. Probeer, waar beschikbaar, verschillende leestbreedtes bij een passende lengte. Kijk of de tenen vrij kunnen liggen en de hiel voldoende blijft zitten. Gebruik geen algemene millimeterregel voor teenruimte als het merk een eigen pasadvies geeft. Verander één onderdeel tegelijk. Vergelijk een andere schoen zonder ook een nieuwe binnenzool of dikker paar sokken toe te voegen. Noteer model, maat en breedteaanduiding. Maak de sluiting alleen zo vast dat de schoen houvast geeft. Meer spanning is geen nuttige test als daardoor direct een drukplek ontstaat. Controleer de verbinding met het pedaal opnieuw. Bij andere schoenen kunnen bevestigingspunten en maatstrepen verschillen. Kopieer daarom niet blind de plaatjesstand. Laat de montage controleren en oefen veilig in- en uitklikken. De bikefitcalculator biedt een algemeen startpunt voor je fietspositie, maar kiest geen passende schoenleest. Vergelijk onder rustige omstandigheden. Test een veilige, passende combinatie twee tot drie rustige ritten. Houd overige afstellingen gelijk en noteer het moment waarop ongemak ontstaat. Stop als de schoen knelt of je gevoel verliest. Ga terug naar de vorige comfortabele combinatie in plaats van het materiaal te laten wennen aan pijn. Waarschuwingssignalen: gevoelloosheid en uitstralende tintelingen zijn redenen om niet door te fietsen. Laat zwelling of pijn in rust of 's nachts medisch beoordelen. Zoek een fitter en zo nodig arts als pijn na drie tot vier zorgvuldige aanpassingen blijft. Een voet die al buiten de fiets klachten geeft, vraagt niet eerst om die hele reeks.
